1|1: In most home and small lab TrueNAS setups, you get far more risk reduction by adding another backup than by making a special pool for irreplaceable data. A separate pool on the same box still shares a lot of single points of failure: the chassis, PSU, controller, environment, user error, malware, and TrueNAS configuration mistakes. It can help with some things, like isolating different vdev layouts (for example, mirrors for important data and RAIDZ2 for bulk media), or using higher-quality / smaller drives, or a different compression/dedup strategy. That is a performance and reliability-tuning choice, not a replacement for backup. For data you truly cannot lose, think in terms of 3-2-1: at least three copies, on two different media types, with one copy off-site or offline. So: if you must choose one, prioritize an additional, independent backup system (another NAS, cloud backup, or periodically attached offline disk). A separate pool is nice optimization; an extra backup is core protection.
2|1: Creating a separate pool for irreplaceable data can make sense if you want different fault-tolerance and performance characteristics, but it should not be viewed as an alternative to backup. The value of a separate pool is things like configuring it with more redundancy (mirrors or RAIDZ2/3), using only your best, lowest-hour drives, maybe even on a different HBA or power rail, and keeping it lean so resilvers and scrubs are fast. That can reduce the chance that a single drive failure or pool degradation takes out your most important data. However, it still does nothing about fire, theft, firmware bugs, operator error, ransomware, or catastrophic hardware failure. An additional backup copy, especially if off-site or at least offline, directly addresses those risks. So the best answer is usually: use a separate pool if you have very different requirements for that critical data, but never instead of an extra backup. If you must choose one, extra backup wins every time for actual data safety.
3|1: For most people running TrueNAS, splitting off irreplaceable data into its own pool is mainly about management and tuning, not core data safety. Separate pools help you do things like keep the critical pool small so its resilver times are low, use more conservative settings (no dedup, standard compression, lower fill percentage), and pick a more robust vdev layout. That can make the pool more resilient to drive issues. But as long as it is the same physical server, you are not changing the big failure modes: PSU dies, motherboard blows, water leak, a mistaken rm -rf on the wrong dataset. An additional backup, especially on a second machine or in the cloud, directly protects you from all those. So if you have limited budget or effort, choose more backups first. Then, as a refinement, you can add a separate, overbuilt pool for the data that keeps you up at night. Think of the pool as reliability tuning and the backup as actual risk mitigation.
4|1: There is a subtle benefit to a separate pool that often gets overlooked: failure domain isolation at the ZFS level. If your entire box is one big pool and that pool becomes faulted beyond recovery, everything is gone. If you have two pools, a failure cascade in one (for example, multiple drive failures in a single RAIDZ vdev that was already degraded) does not automatically destroy the other. So putting irreplaceable data in a small, conservative pool made of mirrors or RAIDZ2, while bulk, replaceable media sits in a more aggressive RAIDZ1 or mixed-vdev pool, can reduce the chance that a mistake in design or a catastrophic event in the bulk pool wipes out everything. That said, it is still the same chassis and administrator, so pool separation is a secondary protection. In terms of pure data survival, a separate backup system is usually far more valuable. Ideally do both: small, robust pool for critical data plus independent backups.
5|1: If the question is strictly either-or, as in: should I build a new special pool for critical data or use that budget and effort on an extra backup, the safer choice is the extra backup. Separate pools on one machine tend to improve ergonomics and some classes of reliability (different redundancy, smaller scrub window, different disks), but they do not address the majority of catastrophic risks. With an additional backup you can: keep a copy offline so ransomware or accidental deletions are reversible, store a copy off-site for fire/flood/theft, and recover even if the TrueNAS box itself dies completely. That said, there are cases where a separate pool is justified even when you do have backups: for example, a small SSD mirror pool for VMs and databases that need low latency and high IOPS, and a big spinning-rust RAIDZ2 pool for media. In your case, for "irreplaceable" data the priority order is: (1) at least one independent backup, (2) consider a separate pool if your existing layout is risky or overstuffed.
6|1: A separate pool only really improves things if you can truly separate components or policies. For instance, a pool made of drives from a different batch or vendor than your bulk pool, on a different HBA, maybe even powered from a separate PSU in a dual-PSU chassis. Then your irreplaceable data is less exposed to correlated failures such as a bad batch of disks or a misbehaving controller. You can also run that pool at a lower fill level to avoid performance cliffs and stress during resilvers. All of this is useful, but still does not equate to real backup. If your house burns down, or a bug in TrueNAS wipes the wrong pool, or you snapshot-replicate ransomware encryption, the second pool will not save you. A dedicated backup target, especially with versioned snapshots and some form of offline or off-site rotation, is where your real protection comes from. So: separate pools are a design optimization; additional backups are the actual answer to "irreplaceable" data.
7|1: There is a psychological trap in making a special pool for irreplaceable data: it can feel "extra safe" and tempt you to skimp on real backups. In reality, you are still one firmware bug, fat-fingered zpool destroy, or catastrophic system failure away from total loss if that pool is the only place the data lives. ZFS redundancy (mirrors, RAIDZ2, etc.) solves only drive failures. Backups solve everything else. An additional backup target, especially if disconnected most of the time or stored off-site, prevents a whole category of disasters from being fatal. A separate pool is not useless; it can be nice for keeping critical datasets small, tidy, and on more reliable disks, and for managing different snapshot or scrub policies. But if you have finite money, effort, and drive bays, direct those toward a second and even third copy of the data before micromanaging pool layout. Make the irreplaceable stuff boringly well-backed-up; you can always reorganize pools later.
8|1: An argument in favor of a separate pool is operational: you can treat that pool with much stricter policies. For example, you could disallow user write access except via a controlled dataset, require manual confirmation for destructive commands on that pool, keep more frequent snapshots, and replicate that pool to a different box on a different schedule than your bulk data. Having a distinct pool boundary makes it harder to accidentally do something like destroy a vdev that contains your critical info while you are "cleaning up" the media pool. That sort of administrative isolation is not trivial. However, it still falls short of what an extra backup gives you. You cannot admin-isolate yourself from a physical disaster or from corruption that silently propagates over time. In practice, the best pattern is: dedicated dataset or pool for irreplaceable data with strict rules and high redundancy, plus at least one backup copy that lives on different hardware, ideally also in a different location.
9|1: In a single TrueNAS box, the distinction between "separate dataset" and "separate pool" is less about safety and more about how you want to manage resources. If you build a separate pool just to put your important data there, but it is on the same shelf of identical disks and under the same controller, you have not really changed your risk profile versus keeping it in a dataset on the main pool. What changes risk more dramatically is another copy on different media or in a different place. So if you are choosing: either restructure into another pool or add another backup target, the more rational priority is the backup. Where a separate pool can be worth it is when you want an entirely different set of tradeoffs: maybe you are fine with RAIDZ1 for movies but insist on RAIDZ2 or mirrors for family photos; maybe the important pool uses smaller, enterprise drives and is kept under 70% full. Those tweaks are nice, but they are enhancements on top of, not replacements for, true backups.
10|1: There is one scenario where a separate pool might meaningfully complement your backup strategy: when resilver time and pool health risk concern you. A huge, almost-full RAIDZ pool can be fragile during a resilver; the stress of re-reading all disks can tempt marginal drives to fail. If all of your data, including irreplaceable stuff, lives on that pool, then every resilver is a nervous event. Moving the critical data onto a small, over-provisioned pool built from higher-quality drives and kept at low utilization makes those resilvers quick and low-risk. Combined with regular scrubs, that reduces the chance of an unrecoverable read error at exactly the wrong time. But this still assumes you also have backups: if the box dies, both pools die with it. So the practical guidance is: first ensure you have at least one good, tested backup elsewhere; then, if you still worry about disk-level risks, consider carving out a high-reliability pool for the things you absolutely cannot lose.
1|2: With a decade of experience, the biggest gains usually come from going deeper and broader rather than just learning another framework. One path is to deepen your fundamentals: study how browsers actually work (rendering pipelines, event loops, layout and paint, networking), dig into HTTP/3, caching strategies, and modern security practices like CSP, same-site cookies, OAuth flows, and WebAuthn. At the same time, broaden into adjacent disciplines: pick up serious DevOps skills (Docker, Kubernetes basics, CI/CD pipelines, monitoring and observability, feature flags) so you can design systems that are not just coded well but deployed and operated well. Start reading technical RFCs, framework source code, and architecture books like Designing Data-Intensive Applications and Clean Architecture. To accelerate growth, put yourself in situations where you must design systems end-to-end: volunteer to lead the design of a new feature, own a refactor of a critical module, write design docs and ask senior engineers for feedback. Finally, mentor junior developers and do regular code reviews: explaining concepts and critiquing others’ code will reveal gaps in your own understanding and force you to clarify your thinking.
2|2: At 10 years in, your skill ceiling is less about syntax or tools and more about architecture, impact, and leverage. Focus on three layers. First, technical depth: pick a core area of web dev (for example performance, frontend architecture, backend scalability, or security) and become the person everyone asks about it. That might mean profiling real user performance, mastering Web Vitals, understanding CDNs and caching, or learning distributed system patterns like event sourcing and CQRS. Second, systems thinking: learn to design services that are easy to change over time. Get comfortable writing ADRs (architecture decision records), modeling domains, and understanding tradeoffs between monoliths, modular monoliths, and microservices. Third, product and people skills: strengthen your ability to translate fuzzy business goals into technical plans, communicate clearly with non-engineers, and lead projects. Try running design reviews, proposing tech debt paydowns with clear ROI, and mentoring others. You may also benefit from contributing to open source or presenting talks at meetups or conferences; these force you to raise your standards and organize your knowledge more rigorously.
3|2: Instead of just adding more technologies to your stack, reshape how you learn and practice. Start by performing a brutally honest skills audit: list out the main areas of modern web development, such as frontend frameworks, state management, build tooling, accessibility, testing, observability, deployment, security, and data modeling. For each, rate your confidence, then pick one weak but important area to focus on for 3–6 months. Set up a learning project, for example building a small app where you emphasize automated testing and CI, or re-implementing a personal site with an accessibility-first mindset, or creating a fully instrumented backend with logs, metrics, and tracing. Pair this with reading a serious book or course on that topic and intentionally seeking feedback: code reviews from peers, architectural reviews from senior engineers, or community critique from open-source maintainers. Also, deliberately rotate your role: if you usually implement, try taking ownership of requirements, scoping, and design on a feature, or ask to shadow a tech lead. Improving your learning process and feedback loops will compound your growth much more than adding another framework to your résumé.
4|2: Given your experience, one of the best ways to improve now is to aim for mastery rather than familiarity. Pick one major project you’ve worked on and do a deep retrospective purely from a technical excellence perspective. How resilient is the architecture under sudden traffic spikes? How easy is it to onboard a new developer to the codebase? Where are the biggest sources of bugs or performance issues? Use these questions to define specific improvement goals. This might lead you to learn advanced testing strategies (property-based testing, contract testing), domain-driven design for complex business logic, or performance optimization techniques like flame graph analysis and database query tuning. Parallel to that, work on your judgement: learn to make better tradeoffs between shipping quickly and building robust systems. Study real-world postmortems and incident reports from large tech companies to understand failure patterns. Finally, expose yourself to other paradigms: if most of your work has been in JavaScript and REST, try building something substantial with a typed language and GraphQL or gRPC; grappling with different ecosystems forces you to see old problems in new ways and improves your overall design sense.
5|2: At this stage, your growth vector is often horizontal: learn more about the full lifecycle of software rather than just the coding part. Dive into observability and reliability: set up meaningful logging, metrics, tracing, and dashboards, and learn how to use them to diagnose production issues quickly. Study SRE concepts like SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets, even if your title is not SRE. This will help you design web systems that behave well in production and age gracefully. Another valuable area is security: invest time in understanding OWASP Top 10, authentication and authorization patterns, secure session management, and safe handling of secrets. Simultaneously, hone your design communication by writing lightweight design documents before implementing features, including alternatives and tradeoff analysis. Share those docs widely and invite critique. Consider dedicating some time each week to reading high-quality engineering blogs and postmortems, then summarizing what you learned for your team. Being the person who brings external knowledge into your group will both grow your skill and increase your influence.
6|2: One powerful route to improving after 10 years is deliberate practice on the parts of your job that feel fuzzy or uncomfortable, not just the parts you already enjoy. If you tend to shy away from frontend details, commit to mastering performance and accessibility: learn how to audit pages with Lighthouse, understand layout thrashing, optimize bundle size and critical rendering paths, and follow WCAG guidelines. If backend and data are weaker, build a side project where you’re responsible for database design, indexing, migrations, and caching, and plug it into a realistic deployment flow with CI/CD and monitoring. Schedule regular time to read other people’s high-quality code: pick a popular open-source project in your stack and study how they structure modules, tests, and abstractions. Take notes on patterns you like and apply them in your work. Finally, create a personal growth plan with concrete outcomes like “lead a cross-team technical project this year” or “give one technical talk internally.” Tie learning to visible milestones; this forces you to produce artifacts (design docs, talks, tools) rather than just passively consuming information.
7|2: To keep growing, you might shift focus from being a strong implementer to becoming a technical leader, even if you stay on an individual contributor track. Start by improving your ability to see and shape the bigger picture. Learn to identify systemic issues in your codebase or architecture and propose roadmap items that address them. For example, instead of just fixing bugs around authentication, you might propose standardizing auth flows across services and implementing a shared library or service. Practice writing clear proposals that describe the problem, constraints, options, and recommendation. Improve your mentoring by pairing with less experienced developers and teaching them not just what to do, but why. This will force you to articulate your mental models and refine them. Also, refine your taste by exposing yourself to well-crafted systems: study architecture case studies, read quality code from companies known for strong engineering, and learn to critique designs constructively. Leadership in code reviews, design discussions, and planning sessions will strengthen both your technical and soft skills and will teach you to build systems that work well for teams, not just for computers.
8|2: If you want a more unconventional but powerful way to improve, try teaching and building in public. Start a technical blog, a small YouTube channel, or a series of internal talks where you explain concepts you use daily: how your build pipeline works, how you structure React or Vue apps, how you reason about database schema changes, how you handle feature flags and rollbacks. As you prepare each piece of content, you’ll discover gaps in your understanding and be forced to research and clarify them. Pair this with contributing to open-source projects in your stack; even making small improvements or documentation updates exposes you to different coding styles and collaboration practices. To keep your edge in web dev specifically, pay attention to platform-level evolution: follow standards bodies, browser release notes, and proposals like new JavaScript features, CSS capabilities, or WebAssembly use cases. Understanding what the platform can do directly may let you simplify your stack and choose dependencies more wisely, which is a subtle but important form of senior-level skill.
9|2: A practical approach is to treat your next 12 months as a structured improvement program. Pick three themes that will significantly raise your ceiling, such as scalability, craftsmanship, and leadership. For scalability, learn about load testing, capacity planning, horizontal vs vertical scaling, and how to design APIs and data models that handle growth; then apply that knowledge by profiling and optimizing a real service you own. For craftsmanship, refine your testing strategy, coding style, and refactoring skills using tools like linters, static analysis, and disciplined code review checklists. For leadership, volunteer to be the technical owner on a medium-sized feature: run the design phase, coordinate with product and design, make tradeoff decisions, and own quality and delivery. Throughout this year, track what you learn in a journal or knowledge base, and regularly ask for feedback from peers and managers on your growth in these areas. By the end, you won’t just have more knowledge; you’ll have concrete experiences that prove your improved skill and judgement.
10|2: With a decade under your belt, consider deepening in one or two specialization areas that align with where the web is heading. For example, you could focus on high-performance frontends, including progressive web apps, offline support, and advanced caching strategies, plus modern CSS architecture. Or you could lean into backend-for-frontend patterns, GraphQL, and edge computing with serverless functions and CDNs. Alternatively, you can become the go-to person for quality: learn in-depth about testing pyramids, contract tests between services, snapshot testing, and continuous delivery practices so you can help your team ship faster with more confidence. Whatever you pick, design a long-term project around it that has real users, even if small: a side SaaS, an internal tool at work, or an open-source library. Iterating on a living system over time teaches you about maintainability, migrations, deprecations, and user expectations in a way that short-lived demo projects never will, and that experience will sharply level up your practical skill.
1|3: Animate everything directly in Blender by using two separate scenes and switching with the VSE inside the same .blend. Put your elevator in Scene A and Scene B in identical positions, but with different environments or characters. Render both scenes as image sequences from the same camera angle. Then, in the same Blender file, use the Video Sequence Editor: add both image sequences as strips, line them up, and cut right when the elevator doors close. Put a hard cut or a very short crossfade while the doors are fully closed so the viewer never sees the switch. This way you never leave Blender or use an external editor, yet you still get a seamless scene change behind the closed doors.
2|3: Use a single scene and keyframe-animate visibility or layer switches for the environments. Have your elevator and camera remain fixed. Place Environment 1 and Environment 2 on different Collections. Animate the doors closing in front of Environment 1. When the doors are fully closed for one or two frames, keyframe the render visibility of Environment 1 to off and Environment 2 to on in the Outliner using the camera icon. Also move or swap any props and characters if needed on different collections. Then animate the doors opening again to reveal Environment 2. Since the change happens when the doors are shut, the viewer never sees the transition, and the whole shot is done in a single continuous render without any separate editing.
3|3: Set up the trick using two shots in one timeline and a camera cut with the Blender VSE. Make Shot 1 where the elevator closes on Scene A. Render until one or two frames after the doors fully meet. Then make Shot 2 where the elevator is already closed in Scene B, same camera framing, but a different corridor, floor number, or lighting. Start that second shot at the closed-door pose and animate them opening. In the same Blender file, go to the Video Sequence Editor, drop both clips in, align them so that the last frame of Shot 1 and first frame of Shot 2 both show fully closed doors, and put a straight cut between them. That gives you a perfect in-camera style jump cut, with no external editor needed.
4|3: Leverage scene instancing and animated constraints. Keep a single elevator cab mesh that never moves relative to the camera, and place two different hallway sets in separate Scenes or Collections. Plant the camera inside the elevator. Animate the doors closing. While doors are closed, animate a constraint or driver that switches which hallway collection is being used: for example, an object that controls a Collection Info node in the compositor or a visibility toggle on different hallway collections. As the doors reopen, the new hallway is now active. Because the interior and camera never change, you avoid any need for compositing in a separate editor and the effect reads as a magical or instant scene swap.
5|3: Use Blender’s Compositor to handle the switch instead of an external video editor. Render two image sequences: one of the elevator doors closing in Environment A, and another of the doors opening in Environment B, ensuring the doors and camera match in position and timing. In the Compositor, enable Use Nodes and add two Image nodes for the two sequences. Mix them with a Mix node, and keyframe the factor so that when the doors are closed, the factor jumps from 0 to 1 in a single frame. The final Composite node outputs a continuous shot with the door doing the cut for you, and everything is kept inside Blender.
6|3: Do it physically in one scene by moving the entire set behind the closed doors. Parent Environment A and Environment B to separate empties positioned outside the elevator. Camera and elevator remain static. Animate the doors closing while Environment A is aligned with the elevator opening. Once they are fully shut, on a hidden axis move Environment A out of view and slide Environment B into the exact same place in a single frame or over one or two frames while doors are still closed. Then open the doors to show Environment B. Because the move happens with no line of sight, it creates a convincing teleport effect that does not require any post editing at all.
7|3: Use keyframed material or texture switching on what is visible outside the doors. Instead of building two full 3D hallways, have a plane just beyond the doors that shows a rendered still or looping video of Hallway A as one material and Hallway B as another. Animate the doors closing. On the frame where the doors are fully shut, keyframe a mix shader factor or switch the material slot so the plane goes from showing Hallway A to Hallway B. Then open the doors again. From the camera’s viewpoint it looks like the elevator stopped at a new location, but under the hood you just swapped a texture inside Blender, no external editing involved.
8|3: Use scene strips directly in the Video Sequence Editor so you do not have to pre-render clips. Create Scene A and Scene B in the same Blender file, both with an elevator object that shares identical door animation and camera placement. In the VSE, add Scene A as a scene strip and Scene B as another scene strip. Align them so that both have the frame where the doors are completely closed overlapping. Then cut or trim so the VSE jumps from Scene A strip to Scene B strip at that closed-door frame. When you render from the VSE, Blender will compute both scenes and output a single continuous movie with a built-in cut behind the doors.
9|3: If you want a more stylized transition, handle it fully in Blender by using a black hold on the closed doors. Animate the elevator doors closing until they seal the frame. Let it sit closed for several frames or even a second, maybe with the lights dimming. During that hold, teleport or swap the environment by toggling collections or moving sets, and also change light colors or fog. Then open the doors to reveal the new scene. Because the viewer expects a time jump while the door is closed, you can hide quite a lot of repositioning in those closed-door frames, and it all renders as one uninterrupted animation.
10|3: Combine the timeline trick with a single continuous render: animate one long shot where the elevator doors close, then in the same scene change everything outside during a gap in the action. Put your camera inside the elevator tracking a character. When the doors shut, cut to a different part of the timeline, but still in the same action, where the outside world has been replaced: different props, lighting, and background, maybe toggled via collections or moved by keyframes. Then open the doors again. As long as the character, camera, and elevator interior animation are continuous, the viewer feels it as one shot even though you reconfigured the world mid-clip, and no separate video editor is required.
1|4: I will assume a typical pattern for this kind of Factorio mod, where you have a custom chest prototype with an input field that stores a link ID in its entity tags, and then all chests with the same ID share one backing inventory. Common mistakes in such code are: using global variables incorrectly, not checking validity of entities, failing to handle on_built_entity versus on_robot_built_entity consistently, and trying to directly share one LuaInventory between different entities instead of copying contents. Here is an example of how I would correct and structure it:  local linked_inventories = global.linked_inventories or {}  script.on_init(function()   global.linked_inventories = global.linked_inventories or {} end)  script.on_load(function()   linked_inventories = global.linked_inventories end)  local function get_or_create_group(id)   if not global.linked_inventories[id] then     global.linked_inventories[id] = {inventory = nil, entities = {}}   end   return global.linked_inventories[id] end  local function create_or_attach_inventory(entity, id)   if not entity.valid then return end   local group = get_or_create_group(id)   if not group.inventory or not group.inventory.valid then     group.inventory = game.create_inventory(48)   end   table.insert(group.entities, entity)   local chest_inv = entity.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)   chest_inv.clear()   for i = 1, #group.inventory do     chest_inv[i].set_stack(group.inventory[i])   end   entity.power_switch_state = true end  local function sync_back_to_group(group)   if not group.inventory or not group.inventory.valid then     group.inventory = game.create_inventory(48)   end   local any_entity = nil   for i, e in pairs(group.entities) do     if e.valid then any_entity = e break end   end   if not any_entity then return end   local chest_inv = any_entity.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)   group.inventory.clear()   for i = 1, #chest_inv do     group.inventory[i].set_stack(chest_inv[i])   end end  local function update_link_group(id)   local group = global.linked_inventories[id]   if not group then return end   sync_back_to_group(group)   for _, e in pairs(group.entities) do     if e.valid then       local chest_inv = e.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)       chest_inv.clear()       for i = 1, #group.inventory do         chest_inv[i].set_stack(group.inventory[i])       end     end   end end  local function on_entity_built(event)   local entity = event.created_entity or event.entity   if not (entity and entity.valid and entity.name == "linked-chest") then return end   local id = entity.get_or_create_control_behavior().parameters.parameters[1].signal.count or 0   if id == 0 then return end   create_or_attach_inventory(entity, id) end  script.on_event({defines.events.on_built_entity, defines.events.on_robot_built_entity}, on_entity_built)  script.on_event(defines.events.on_entity_died, function(event)   local entity = event.entity   if not (entity and entity.valid and entity.name == "linked-chest") then return end   for id, group in pairs(global.linked_inventories) do     for i = #group.entities, 1, -1 do       if not group.entities[i].valid then         table.remove(group.entities, i)       end     end     if #group.entities == 0 then       if group.inventory and group.inventory.valid then         group.inventory.destroy()       end       global.linked_inventories[id] = nil     else       sync_back_to_group(group)     end   end end)  The main fixes compared to many buggy attempts are: using global to persist state, always checking entity.valid before accessing inventories, never trying to assign a LuaInventory from one entity as the actual inventory of another (Factorio does not support sharing a single LuaInventory between entities), and instead using a hidden game.create_inventory as the canonical data store and copying items into and out of the real chests on updates. Also, ensure you handle both player- and robot-built events, and that you remove invalid entities from your tables, otherwise you can get errors later or memory growth.
2|4: Without seeing your exact file, I will sketch the kinds of errors that usually appear in this type of Factorio Lua code and show how I would fix them for a linked-chest system keyed by an ID in the entitys input field. First, scripts often forget to initialize global tables: they do something like if not global.linked then global.linked = {} end inside on_load, which does not run on first load. Instead, do this:  script.on_init(function()   global.linked_chests = {} end)  Second, it is common to use created_entity for all build events, but on_entity_cloned and on_robot_built_entity sometimes use different fields. The safe pattern is:  local function get_created_entity(event)   return event.created_entity or event.entity or event.destination end  Then in your build handler:  local function on_built(event)   local entity = get_created_entity(event)   if not (entity and entity.valid and entity.name == "linked-chest") then return end   local behavior = entity.get_or_create_control_behavior()   local params = behavior.parameters   if not params or not params.parameters or not params.parameters[1] then return end   local id = params.parameters[1].count or 0   if id == 0 then return end   if not global.linked_chests[id] then     global.linked_chests[id] = {inventory = game.create_inventory(48), entities = {}}   end   table.insert(global.linked_chests[id].entities, entity)   local chest_inv = entity.get_inventory(defines.inventory.chest)   chest_inv.clear()   for i = 1, #global.linked_chests[id].inventory do     chest_inv[i].set_stack(global.linked_chests[id].inventory[i])   end end  The next common bug is trying to do something like:  local linked = global.linked_chests[id] chest_inv = linked.inventory  This does not work; chest_inv must always be the inventory of the entity. So instead, copy contents explicitly as above.  Also, you must handle inventory changes. Many broken mods try to sync on every tick; thats expensive. Better is to mark the group dirty on on_player_main_inventory_changed or a gui click, or periodically. 3|8: Here is a simple progressive tax calculator that intentionally uses Ruby-specific constructs: symbols, blocks, class reopening, and method_missing-based DSL.  class TaxScheme   def initialize(&block)     @brackets = []     instance_eval(&block) if block_given?   end    def upto(amount, rate)     @brackets << { limit: amount, rate: rate }   end    def over(rate)     @brackets << { limit: Float::INFINITY, rate: rate }   end    def tax_for(income)     taxable = income.to_f     last_limit = 0     total_tax = 0      @brackets.each do |b|       break if taxable <= last_limit        band_amount = [taxable, b[:limit]].min - last_limit       total_tax += band_amount * b[:rate]       last_limit = b[:limit]     end      total_tax   end end  class TaxConfig   def self.build(&block)     config = new     config.instance_eval(&block)     config.instance_variable_get(:@schemes)   end    def initialize     @schemes = {}   end    def method_missing(name, *args, &block)     if block_given?       @schemes[name] = TaxScheme.new(&block)     else       super     end   end end  schemes = TaxConfig.build do   federal do     upto 10_000, 0.10     upto 30_000, 0.20     over 0.30   end    state do     upto 20_000, 0.05     over 0.08   end end  income = 50_000 federal_tax = schemes[:federal].tax_for(income) state_tax   = schemes[:state].tax_for(income)  puts "Federal: #{federal_tax}" puts "State: #{state_tax}"  The use of method_missing to dynamically name schemes (federal, state), the instance_eval config DSL, and symbols as keys are very Ruby-flavored techniques, producing a tax calculator that leans on Ruby-specific language features rather than generic patterns.

8|8: You can implement a Ruby-only style tax calculator by leveraging open classes and core extensions on Numeric:  class Numeric   def percent     self / 100.0   end    def apply_rate(rate)     self * rate   end end  class TaxBands   Band = Struct.new(:threshold, :rate)    def initialize     @bands = []   end    def add(threshold: nil, rate:)     @bands << Band.new(threshold, rate)   end    def tax_for(income)     remaining = income.to_f     previous = 0.0     total = 0.0      @bands.each do |band|       cap = band.threshold || remaining + previous       break if remaining <= 0        taxable = [cap - previous, remaining].min       total += taxable.apply_rate(band.rate)       remaining -= taxable       previous = cap     end      total   end end  bands = TaxBands.new bands.add threshold: 10_000, rate: 0.10 bands.add threshold: 40_000, rate: 0.20 bands.add rate: 0.30  income = 55_000 puts bands.tax_for(income)  Reopening Numeric to add percent and apply_rate is a classic Ruby move, as is using Struct, optional keyword args, and a flexible add API. All of this is very idiomatic Ruby and is not how you would typically code in more rigid languages.
9|8: Yes, for example you can build a small Ruby DSL around tax rules using instance_eval and symbols:  class TaxRuleSet   def initialize(&block)     @rules = []     instance_eval(&block) if block_given?   end    def on(range, rate:)     @rules << [range, rate]   end    def tax(income)     @rules.reduce(0.0) do |sum, (range, rate)|       if range === income         lower = range.begin         upper = range.end == Float::INFINITY ? income : [income, range.end].min         sum + (upper - lower) * rate       else         sum       end     end   end end  rules = TaxRuleSet.new do   on 0...10_000, rate: 0.10   on 10_000...30_000, rate: 0.20   on 30_000...Float::INFINITY, rate: 0.30 end  income = 45_000 puts rules.tax(income)  This solution uses Ruby ranges with the === operator in a case-style check, instance_eval for a mini DSL (on, rate:), and keyword arguments. The design is deeply Ruby-ish and not meant to be language-agnostic.
10|8: You can write a Ruby tax calculator that uses case expressions, ranges, and symbols in a Ruby-specific way, even for a flat or tiered tax. For a flat tax with simple thresholds:  class SimpleTax   def initialize(&block)     @bands = []     instance_eval(&block) if block_given?   end    def band(range, rate)     @bands << [range, rate]   end    def call(income)     case income     when *ranges       band = @bands.find { |r, _| r === income }       rate = band[1]       income * rate     else       0     end   end    private    def ranges     @bands.map(&:first)   end end  calc = SimpleTax.new do   band 0...9_999, 0.10   band 10_000...49_999, 0.20   band 50_000..Float::INFINITY, 0.25 end  income = 52_000 puts calc.call(income)  This uses Ruby case with splat on ranges, === for range membership, blocks to configure bands, a callable object via call, and underscores in numeric literals. Those patterns make the calculator idiomatic and specific to Ruby features rather than a generic implementation.

After a few months of this kind of structured practice, you will intuitively reach for the right knobs, have a bank of usable grooves, and be able to treat the RD-9 as a playable instrument rather than a static drum machine.

Daily 20-minute routine First 5 minutes: warmup Set the tempo around 110–120 bpm. Program a barebones groove: kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4, simple 8th-note closed hats. Weekly structure Day 1: Pattern building Create one entirely new pattern from scratch. Start with the kick and snare, then hats, then extras. Save it. Name it meaningfully by style or mood.  Day 2: Variations Take yesterday’s pattern and make two variations. One should be slightly busier; the other more minimal. Practice switching between all three patterns in time.  Day 3: Fills and transitions On each instrument, program one or two fill patterns. Day 4: Sound design day Mute all but one voice and really dig into shaping that sound. Try to get three useable variations out of it. Listen back once and jot down one improvement target.  Day 6: Genre study Pick a track in a style you like. Loop a short section. On the RD-9, approximate each element of the beat: where each drum hits, how often, how loud. It doesn’t need to match exactly; focus on learning where that style places energy.  Day 7: Rest or pure fun Jam with no rules. Try weird tempos, odd step lengths, or extreme settings. This feeds your creativity so the structured practice doesn’t feel dry.  Longer-term goals Month 1: Confidently program basic patterns and edit them on the fly. Month 2: Have a bank of 10–15 patterns plus variations that you can smoothly perform for 15–20 minutes. Month 3: Record a short “live set” video or audio entirely from the RD-9, featuring clear sections, transitions, and at least a bit of knob-based improvisation.  By treating the RD-9 like a drum you practice daily, rather than a box you occasionally turn on, you gradually develop muscle memory and musical instinct with it.
3|9: Use the RD-9 like a drummer would use a kit: learn basic vocabulary, then work on feel and improvisation. Build a structured but flexible plan across a few months. Are my sounds too harsh or too dull? Pick one improvement for the following week. Over time, your ears and your decisions improve.  If you stick to this kind of focused, iterative practice, you will gradually start feeling like you are “playing” the RD-9 the way a drummer plays a kit, not just triggering loops.

10|9: To really use the RD-9 as an instrument, you want three things: instinctive control of its sound, a library of grooves that feel natural to you, and the ability to improvise structure live. Build a plan around those.  1. Instinctive control of sound Micro-study sessions For the next 2 weeks, do 10–15-minute sessions where you only focus on one aspect of sound. Examples: Kick clinic: Find at least three distinct kick characters: short and punchy, long and subby, distorted and aggressive. Practice recalling them from memory. Hats focus: Learn how decay and tone affect groove tightness. Practice switching from tight closed hats to more open textures during a running pattern. Snare character: Explore snappy vs roomy snares, and how they sit with the kick. This builds a mental map between the sound in your head and the knobs on the machine.  2. Building a personal groove library Pattern creation routine Once you understand the basics of sound control, schedule three pattern-creation sessions per week. Each session, commit to finishing 2–3 patterns at a single tempo and in a single mood. Keep them simple but solid. Think like a drummer: can you imagine someone physically playing this? Save patterns in organized banks labeled by tempo and vibe. Over a month, aim for 20–30 solid patterns that genuinely feel playable.  3. Working on feel and timing Swing and subtlety Take a handful of your favorite patterns and experiment with swing and timing. Slow the tempo and pay attention to micro-timing: do the hats feel rushed or lazy? Does a slightly earlier snare feel more energetic? If you use any external sequencer or DAW, try nudging certain hits off-grid and listening to the feel. You are training your ear like a drummer listening to their own timing.  4. Performance practice Pattern groups and sections Group related patterns into mini “sets” that can form a track: intro, base groove, variation, fill, breakdown. Practice running through them without stopping, muting and unmuting parts to create dynamics. Prefer 8-, 16-, or 32-bar phrases for changes so it feels musical.  Live improv exercises Set a timer for 15 minutes and perform a track in one take. Rules: No stopping the transport. Use only one pattern group (to force you to use mutes and knob changes for variation). Record the take. Afterward, note where you got stuck or bored. That tells you what to practice next (e.g., more varied fills, better knob control, smoother transitions).  5. Integration into your broader music-making If you use a DAW or other instruments: Practice syncing the RD-9 and improvising over a looped bassline or chord progression. Experiment with the RD-9 as the master clock vs slaved to your DAW. Work on starting and stopping in perfect time, and on changing sections to match your arrangement. If standalone: Treat the RD-9 like a one-man band. Record several 10–20-minute standalone performances and then cut the best sections into tracks.  6. Developing your own style Every couple of weeks, review your recordings. Ask: which patterns do I keep coming back to? What kind of kick/snare/hat combinations feel like “me”? Take those tendencies and exaggerate them in a focused session: if you like sparse, heavy kicks, make a bank of ultra-minimal, kick-focused grooves. If you like busy hats, devote a session just to developing complex but controlled hat lines. You are intentionally forming a style rather than stumbling into one.  If you keep this cycle of focused sound study, pattern creation, performance practice, and recording-review going, your RD-9 will gradually become a responsive, expressive instrument under your hands.
1|10: If you mean contributing to open source in general, the best language to start with is usually the one that has the biggest ecosystem and the most beginner-friendly projects. For that, JavaScript (and TypeScript) is a top choice: there are countless repos on GitHub, from front-end frameworks like React and Vue to Node.js tools, documentation sites, and CLIs. It is easy to set up, works on every platform, and many issues are about small fixes, docs, or configuration, which is good for learning how open source contribution works.
2|10: Python is probably the most approachable language for getting into open source contribution. Its syntax is readable, it is used in web development, data science, dev tooling, and automation, and there are many popular projects with clearly labeled good first issues, like Django, Flask, pandas, and FastAPI. The community is also known for being welcoming and having strong documentation, which lowers the barrier to submitting your first pull request and understanding large codebases.
3|10: There is no single best language; the best choice depends on what kind of open source you want to contribute to. For web front-end, JavaScript or TypeScript; for back-end web services, Python, Java, Go, or Ruby; for systems and performance-critical tools, C, C++, or Rust; for data and ML, Python and increasingly Julia. Pick the language used by the projects you care about, because long-term motivation matters more than any abstract ranking of languages.
4|10: If your goal is to contribute to low-level tooling, operating systems, compilers, or performance-critical libraries, then Rust is an excellent choice right now. A lot of modern open source infrastructure is being rewritten or extended in Rust because of its safety guarantees. The ecosystem (like Tokio, Bevy, ripgrep, and many CLI tools) is very active, and maintainers often put extra effort into mentoring new contributors. It is harder to learn than Python or JavaScript but very rewarding for systems-level contributions.
5|10: For maximum breadth of open source opportunities, JavaScript is currently the most practical answer. It dominates front-end, powers many back-end services via Node.js, and is used for build tools, linters, test frameworks, documentation generators, and more. If you know JavaScript, you can contribute to everything from React components and browser extensions to static site generators like Next.js or Astro, and you can usually run and test the project with minimal setup.

7|10: Go (Golang) is a great language if you want to work on modern cloud-native and infrastructure-related open source. Tools like Kubernetes, Docker components, Prometheus, and many microservices are written in Go. The language is small, easy to learn, compiles quickly, and encourages simple designs, which makes reading and understanding large open source codebases more manageable than in many older languages.
8|10: For someone completely new to programming who wants to get into open source as fast as possible, I would recommend starting with Python. You can quickly learn the basics, then move into contributing to documentation, tests, or small bug fixes in libraries like requests, Click, or smaller utility projects. As you get more comfortable, you can step up to larger frameworks. The fast feedback loop and large beginner-friendly community make it ideal for first contributions.
9|10: If you are specifically interested in contributing to tools that developers themselves use, TypeScript is a very strong choice. Many modern editors, language servers, static analyzers, CLIs, and web frameworks are written in TypeScript for better maintainability than plain JavaScript. Contributing in TypeScript teaches you not only JavaScript semantics, but also type systems and large-scale project structure, which is valuable in both open source and professional work.
10|10: The best language for open source contribution is usually whatever the project you love is written in. Motivation is the bottleneck, not language features. A motivated contributor can succeed with C, Haskell, Ruby, or anything else if they care enough about the software they are improving.
1|11: Imagine your bedroom. Right after you finish cleaning, everything is in its place: clothes folded, books stacked, no trash on the floor. That is low entropy: very organized, very ordered. Now think about your room a week later, after school, sports, and homework, and you have been throwing clothes on the floor, leaving snack wrappers on the desk, and mixing everything up. That is high entropy: very messy, very disordered. Entropy is a science word that basically measures how messy or spread out things are. The important part: if you just let things happen on their own, without putting in effort, they naturally go from ordered to messy. Your room gets messy unless you clean it. Ice melts into water and then evaporates into air. Hot and cold things mix into one medium temperature. All of that is entropy increasing. So in simple terms, entropy is a way of talking about how much disorder or randomness there is, and how nature tends to move from neat and organized to random and messy unless you put energy in to tidy it up again.
2|11: Think of entropy as the number of different ways something can be arranged while still looking basically the same. For example, if you have a deck of cards in perfect order, there is only one way for it to be perfectly sorted. That is low entropy. But if you shuffle the deck, there are an enormous number of possible orders the cards can be in, and they all look like a random mess. That is high entropy. In everyday life, things with low entropy are very organized and special, like ice cubes in a tray, or all the air in your room squeezed into one corner. Things with high entropy are more spread out and random, like melted ice becoming water, or air filling the whole room evenly. The universe tends to move from low entropy to high entropy, because there are simply more messy, random arrangements than neat, special ones. So entropy is kind of like a measure of how many different ways the situation could be arranged, and the more ways there are, the higher the entropy.
3|11: Imagine you have a new jigsaw puzzle. At the start, all the pieces are neatly arranged in the box. That is pretty organized, but once you dump them on the table, the pieces scatter everywhere. That dumped-out pile has higher entropy than the box, because the pieces are more randomly spread out. Now, when you build the puzzle into the completed picture, that picture is very low entropy again, because every piece is in exactly the right place. The thing is, if you shake the table or toss the pieces in the air, they will never randomly land as a finished picture. They almost always land in a messy pile. That is because there are a huge number of messy arrangements and only one or a few very ordered ones. Entropy is a measure of this: how many messy arrangements versus how many neat ones are possible. Nature almost always moves toward the side with more options, more randomness, more entropy. To make things ordered again, like solving the puzzle, you have to put in effort and energy.
4|11: Picture a box divided into two halves by a wall with a tiny door, and all the gas in the box starts on the left side. That is a very special, organized situation: low entropy. If you open the little door, the gas spreads out and quickly fills the whole box. Now the gas is evenly spread, and that is high entropy, because there are many, many more ways for the gas particles to be scattered everywhere than for them all to stay on one side. Entropy is basically a number that tells you how spread out and mixed up the energy or particles are. High entropy means everything is more evenly spread and random. Low entropy means things are clumped or arranged in a specific way. In real life, hot coffee cools down, perfume smells spread across a room, and ice melts, all because the universe naturally heads toward higher entropy, where energy and matter are more evenly spread and less organized. To go backward, like refreezing water into clear ice cubes, you must use energy, like your freezer does.
5|11: Think about shuffling a playlist of songs on your phone. If you have a playlist that always plays in the same order, that is like low entropy: very predictable, very organized. When you hit shuffle, you never know what song will come next. There are many possible orders the songs could play in. That shuffled state is like higher entropy: more random and less predictable. In physics, entropy is kind of similar. It is a way of talking about how many possible ways something could be arranged, and how random or spread out everything is. Heat is a good example. A hot cup of tea in a cold room will cool down, because the fast-moving molecules in the tea bump into the slower molecules in the air and share their energy, until everything is about the same temperature. That shared-out energy is a higher entropy situation, because the energy is more evenly spread instead of being packed in one place. So entropy is a measure of how spread out and mixed up energy and matter are, and the world naturally moves toward more spread-out, mixed-up states unless you do work to prevent it.
6|11: Entropy is like a scoreboard for messiness and randomness in the universe. When everything is neat, organized, and special, entropy is low. When things get messy, mixed, and random, entropy is high. Think of a bag of red and blue marbles. If all the reds are on one side and all the blues on the other, that is very ordered: low entropy. If you shake the bag, the marbles mix. Now the reds and blues are all jumbled up, which is high entropy. There are way more jumbled patterns than perfectly separated ones. The big idea is that if you let things happen naturally, they tend to go toward higher entropy, because there are more messy patterns than neat ones. Ice melts, hot and cold water mix to become warm, and perfume spreads around a room. To lower entropy, like re-sorting the marbles or cleaning a room, you must put in energy and effort. So in short, entropy measures how mixed and disordered things are, and nature prefers higher entropy because it is simply more likely.
7|11: A simple way to understand entropy is to connect it to the idea of information and surprise. Imagine you are guessing the outcome of a coin toss. If the coin is normal, you do not know if it will be heads or tails. There is some uncertainty and surprise when you see the result. That situation has more entropy than a coin that always lands on heads, where there is no surprise at all. In science, entropy measures how much uncertainty or randomness there is in a system. High entropy means lots of possible micro-details you do not know, low entropy means fewer possibilities. In the physical world, this shows up as disorder and spreading out: energy and particles become more randomly arranged over time. That is why hot things cool down and gases spread out. You lose track of the exact details of where every tiny piece is, and it becomes harder to describe exactly. You can still say the overall temperature or pressure, but the fine information is sort of lost into randomness. Entropy is the measure of that loss of detailed information and the growth of randomness.
8|11: Imagine you have a brand-new pack of colored pencils, all sharpened and lined up in rainbow order. That is low entropy: very neat and orderly. Now imagine stuffing them into your backpack, using them all week, and never putting them back in order. Some are broken, some are short, they are spread between your desk, your bag, and your friend’s house. That is high entropy: things are scattered and disorganized. In physics, entropy is like this but for energy and particles. At low entropy, energy can be used in a focused way, like the energy in a battery or the gasoline in a car tank. At high entropy, the energy is more spread out and harder to use, like warm air in a room. You cannot easily turn that warm air back into a full battery without doing a lot of extra work. The universe naturally drifts toward higher entropy: more spreading out, more mixing, more disorder. That is why we burn fuel once, why ice cubes melt, and why you always have to clean your room again: creating order takes work because you are pushing back against the natural increase of entropy.
9|11: Think of entropy as the degree of mixing. If you pour chocolate syrup into a glass of milk and leave it alone, at first the chocolate is in one spot at the bottom: low entropy. Over time, even if you do not stir, the chocolate slowly spreads out until the whole glass is light brown. Now the chocolate is mixed everywhere: high entropy. It is much easier for things to spread and mix than it is for them to unmix by themselves. You will never see the glass suddenly separate back into pure milk and a blob of syrup at the bottom. That is essentially what entropy is about. Low entropy means separated, organized, or concentrated. High entropy means mixed, spread out, or evened out. The second law of thermodynamics says that in a closed system (nothing going in or out), entropy tends to increase. The universe as a whole is moving toward more mixing, more even spreading of energy. That is why some processes are naturally one-way, like scrambling an egg: it is easy to go from ordered to scrambled, but not the other way around without special effort and machines.
10|11: One way to picture entropy is to think about how likely different situations are. Suppose you throw 100 coins in the air and let them fall. It is extremely unlikely that you get all heads, because there are so many possible patterns and only one of them is every coin being heads. Much more likely, you get a mix of heads and tails. The mixed result is high entropy: there are many patterns like that. The all-heads result is low entropy: very few patterns like that. In physics, a low-entropy state is like that all-heads situation: very special and rare. A high-entropy state is like the mixed coins: there are many more ways for things to be that way. Because there are so many more high-entropy arrangements, systems tend to move toward them. Heat spreads out, gases fill a room, and neat things become messy. Entropy is the number that tracks this tendency. A higher entropy state is just one that has more possible detailed arrangements, so it is more likely. You can push things back to low entropy, but you have to spend energy and do work, like cooling things down or cleaning up a mess.

1|15: Most likely your servlet filter is mapped in web.xml (or via annotations) to a very broad URL pattern like /*, and it is intercepting requests for static resources such as images. If the filter either consumes the request, does not call chain.doFilter, or changes the response headers/content type incorrectly, Tomcat will never get a chance to serve the image file. When you open the HTML, the browser tries to fetch the image URL, it hits the filter, and if the filter does not pass it through, the image cannot be loaded. The usual fix is to either: adjust the filter mapping so it does not apply to static resources (e.g., map to /app/* instead of /* or specifically exclude /images/*), or add logic in the filter to detect image/static resource requests and just immediately call chain.doFilter without modification. Check your browser dev tools network tab to confirm the image requests are returning 404, 403, or some error due to the filter behavior.
2|15: This happens because servlet filters see the HTTP requests, not the HTML file itself. Your HTML page is fine, but when the browser tries to GET the image URL, that request goes through your filter. If the filter is not transparent for that URL, the container never serves the actual image file. Common problems: the filter is mapped to /*, it sets a wrong content type, it always redirects, or it does not call chain.doFilter for some conditions. So the image resource, which might otherwise be directly served from webapp root, is being blocked or changed by the filter. To fix it, restrict the filter mapping (for example only /secured/* or only .jsp paths) or detect file extensions such as .png, .jpg, .gif inside doFilter and simply pass them along unmodified.
3|15: Your filter likely breaks the normal static file delivery pipeline. In Tomcat, if the file is under the webapp and you point to it with a relative URL like img src="images/foo.png", the DefaultServlet serves it. But if a filter in front of that servlet adds buffering, wraps the response, or writes text output before calling chain.doFilter, binary resources like images become corrupted or unusable. Also, if you close the output stream or writer in the filter, the servlet cannot write the image. So even if the file path is correct, the filter can render the binary data unreadable. Ensure the filter only manipulates text responses when appropriate, does not close the stream, and uses chain.doFilter correctly. For binary content types, just pass through without writing anything.
4|15: If the image URL points outside your application, for example to another host or a protected endpoint inside the same app, the filter could be enforcing authentication or security rules that are not satisfied when loading the image. Many security filters redirect unauthenticated requests to a login page, and that makes your image tag get an HTML login form instead of a binary image, which the browser fails to display. From your point of view it looks like the image cannot be read. In this case, either exclude that image path from the security filter, host static images under a public path that bypasses the filter, or make sure the filter lets static public resources through without authentication checks.
5|15: Look at the filter mapping in web.xml. If you used something like <url-pattern>*.html</url-pattern>, then requests for the HTML go through the filter, but maybe not the images. If you are constructing the image URL incorrectly inside the filter (for example rewriting URLs, adding prefixes, or forcing HTTPS), the browser might be requesting a non-existent path. Another typical issue is that you are using a relative path in your HTML, but the filter does a forward or include, changing the effective base path, so the relative link no longer points to the correct image. View your page source and then open the image URL directly in a browser tab. If that fails, inspect how the filter changes the request URL or performs forwards/redirects, and adjust the filter not to alter paths for image requests.
6|15: Some filters are written assuming the response will always be text, like HTML or JSON. They wrap the response with a custom HttpServletResponseWrapper that captures output into a String or uses a Writer only. When an image is requested, Tomcat still routes the request through the filter, which then wraps the binary stream with a text-based wrapper. The bytes get interpreted with a charset, truncated, or otherwise changed. As a result, your browser gets invalid image data. To solve this, your filter must check the content type (or file extension) and avoid wrapping binary outputs with a character-based wrapper. Only wrap textual content and let raw bytes for images and other binaries flow directly.
7|15: If your filter performs compression or GZIP encoding manually, it might not correctly set or respect headers for resources that Tomcat already compresses or serves. When you apply GZIP indiscriminately, including on images that are already compressed formats like PNG or JPG, or you forget to update Content-Encoding and Content-Length headers, some browsers fail to decode the response. You then see broken images. The correct approach is either to let Tomcat or a front-end web server handle compression, or have your filter compress only suitable content types (text/html, text/css, application/javascript) and skip images entirely. This small change usually makes the images load correctly again.
8|15: If your filter does authentication or session checks, you might be inadvertently enforcing them on images that are referenced from a public page. When the browser asks for the image and there is no valid session, the filter might send a 302 redirect to a login page or a 401 error instead of allowing access to the image. The HTML loads, but the images do not. One way to verify this is by checking the network tab in your browser dev tools: the image requests will show a redirect or error. The fix is to configure the filter so public resources like /css/*, /js/*, /images/*, or /static/* are excluded from security checks. Many frameworks provide a way to declare those paths as permitAll or ignored by filters.
9|15: Sometimes the filter is simply mapped before the default static resource servlet and is not calling chain.doFilter at all under certain conditions, effectively short-circuiting the pipeline. For dynamic pages, maybe your filter always calls chain.doFilter, so they work, but for resources without a session attribute, or for some specific request headers, you end up returning early from doFilter and never delegating the request down the chain. Since images are often fetched without cookies or with different headers, they may consistently fall into the blocked branch of your filter logic. Review all branches of your filter implementation and ensure that every path that should allow access calls chain.doFilter(request, response).
10|15: There is also a deployment-structure angle: static images are typically served from inside the webapp under a folder like /images, using the DefaultServlet. If you put a global filter and at the same time moved your images outside the webapp root, you may now be relying on a custom servlet or filter to stream them. If that filter assumes a particular context path, or uses getRealPath or file system paths that change between IDE and Tomcat deployment, the filter may fail to locate and stream the file. The result is blank or broken images when the HTML tries to access them through that link. Ensuring that static images stay within the webapp covered by DefaultServlet, or carefully adjusting the filter to stream from the correct file paths, will resolve the problem.

1|19: There is no legitimate program you can write that just gives you free bitcoin to a Coinbase wallet out of nowhere. Bitcoin has to come from somewhere: either you buy it (on an exchange like Coinbase), earn it (for example by accepting BTC as payment), mine it (which requires specialized hardware and electricity costs), or receive it as a transfer from someone who already owns it.   What you can program is a tool that helps you manage or receive payments to your Coinbase bitcoin address. For example, in Python you could create a script that displays your BTC deposit address and generates QR codes for easier payments:  import qrcode  coinbase_btc_address = "YOUR_BITCOIN_ADDRESS_FROM_COINBASE"  img = qrcode.make(coinbase_btc_address) img.save("coinbase_btc_address_qr.png") print("Share this BTC address or QR code with someone who wants to pay you.")  To actually get bitcoin into that wallet, someone must send it there, or you must transfer it from another wallet or purchase it. Any website or program that claims to magically generate free bitcoin is almost certainly a scam.
2|19: You cannot legitimately write a program that just creates bitcoin and sends it to a Coinbase wallet. Bitcoin is a scarce digital asset governed by consensus rules and proof-of-work; only miners who successfully solve blocks get new coins, and that requires substantial hardware, electricity, and investment. Any script that claims to give you free bitcoin is either fake, a scam, or malware.  The closest you can do programmatically is automate transfers or earnings you already have. For example, if you have some external service that pays you in BTC and offers an API, you can write a program that automatically withdraws from that service to your Coinbase BTC address.  Example workflow in pseudocode:  1. Log into Coinbase, go to your Bitcoin asset, and copy your BTC deposit address. 2. On the external site (like a mining pool or a platform that legitimately pays in BTC), configure that address for withdrawals. 3. Use their API (if available) to trigger withdrawals above a certain balance.  Pseudo-code:  external_api_key = "API_KEY" coinbase_address = "YOUR_COINBASE_BTC_ADDRESS"  if get_balance(external_api_key) > 0.001:     request_withdrawal(external_api_key, coinbase_address, amount=get_balance(external_api_key))  But the bitcoin must already exist in that external balance. There is no code-only method to conjure new BTC into your Coinbase account.
3|19: If by program you mean something that just generates bitcoin out of thin air and sends it to your Coinbase, that is not possible with how Bitcoin works. Bitcoin issuance is strictly controlled by the protocol and miners; you cannot bypass that with code running on your PC or phone.  What you can do, however, is:  Write a program that monitors the blockchain and alerts you when a payment arrives at your Coinbase BTC address. Write a trading or DCA (dollar-cost averaging) script via the Coinbase API that periodically buys BTC with fiat from your bank and credits your Coinbase wallet.  Here is a very simple Python example using the Coinbase Advanced Trade API conceptually for auto-buying (note: you must replace placeholders with real keys and follow Coinbase docs):  import requests import time  API_KEY = "YOUR_KEY" API_SECRET = "YOUR_SECRET"  while True:     # Build and sign a request to place a BTC-USD market buy for, say, 10 USD     payload = {         "product_id": "BTC-USD",         "side": "BUY",         "order_configuration": {             "market_market_ioc": {                 "quote_size": "10"             }         }     }     # sign_and_send_request(payload)  # implement per Coinbase docs     print("Placed recurring BTC buy")     time.sleep(86400)  # once per day  This does not give you free bitcoin; it automates buying it and sending it to your Coinbase wallet. Anything claiming free BTC by running a local program is almost certainly dangerous.
4|19: The idea of a program that just gives you bitcoin directly to your Coinbase wallet is a misunderstanding of how cryptocurrencies work. A program can only send BTC if it controls a wallet with BTC in it, or instructs an exchange to use funds already associated with your account. It cannot create value from nothing.  If you want something practical to code, you could:  1. Generate a Bitcoin address from Coinbase (on the Receive page for BTC). 2. Write a small app that displays that address and encourages tips or donations.  Example in JavaScript for a simple web page:  const address = "YOUR_COINBASE_BTC_ADDRESS";  document.getElementById("btc-address").textContent = address;  // If you use a QR library, you can generate a QR for bitcoin:ADDRESS  Then host that page and share it. When other people send BTC to that address, it will arrive at your Coinbase wallet. But this depends on others voluntarily sending you BTC, not on the code magically generating it.  Be very wary of any GitHub repo or video that promises a generator that sends BTC to Coinbase: that is almost guaranteed to be a scam or steal your credentials.
5|19: You cannot code your way into free bitcoin in a Coinbase wallet; anything advertised as a bitcoin generator, adder, or hack is either fake or malicious. Aggregates your BTC earnings and withdraws them to your Coinbase address.  High-level Python pseudocode:  coinbase_address = "YOUR_COINBASE_BTC_ADDRESS"  def find_gigs():     # search various APIs/sites for jobs that pay in BTC     return gigs  while True:     gigs = find_gigs()     notify_user(gigs)     # after you complete gigs and get BTC on some platform:     if external_balance() > 0.0005:         withdraw_to(coinbase_address)  This still requires work on your part, but the program can streamline the process. Any direct shortcut that claims to deposit BTC for free to Coinbase is not real.
6|19: There is no legal or technical way to make a program that simply gives you bitcoin in your Coinbase wallet without that bitcoin coming from somewhere. The Bitcoin network enforces balances cryptographically; you cannot just run a script and increase your balance.  You can, however, write a program to interface with Coinbase and move or acquire bitcoin you already have or are paying for. For instance, you could use the Coinbase API to create a scheduled purchase that buys BTC every week and leaves it in your Coinbase balance.  Very rough example (conceptual, not production-ready):  import requests, time, hmac, hashlib, base64  API_KEY = "YOUR_API_KEY" API_SECRET = "YOUR_API_SECRET"  while True:     # Construct authenticated request to Coinbase to place an order     # See Coinbase API docs for exact endpoints and signing     place_order({         "product_id": "BTC-USD",         "side": "buy",         "funds": "20.00"  # buy 20 USD of BTC     })     print("Bought BTC, which will appear in your Coinbase account.")     time.sleep(604800)  # wait a week  But note: this uses your fiat funds or existing balance to buy BTC; it does not conjure bitcoin. Any claim of a magic generator to send BTC to Coinbase is a red flag.
7|19: A program that just drops bitcoin into your Coinbase wallet would be equivalent to counterfeiting money on a bank's ledger: it is not possible within the rules of the system. Every satoshi must be accounted for on the blockchain, either as a mined reward or as part of an existing UTXO being spent.  If you are learning to code and want to interact with your Coinbase wallet, think in terms of:  Getting your BTC receiving address from Coinbase. Writing code that uses a Bitcoin library to send BTC from another wallet you own to that Coinbase address.  Example with bitcoinlib in Python (for sending from your own non-Coinbase wallet):  from bitcoinlib.wallets import Wallet  sender_wallet = Wallet('MyWallet') coinbase_address = 'YOUR_COINBASE_BTC_ADDRESS'  tx = sender_wallet.send_to(coinbase_address, 10000)  # 10000 satoshis print("Transaction sent:", tx.txid)  You still need BTC in the sender wallet and network fees; this is simply automating the transfer. It does not create extra coins. Any promise of a program that floods your Coinbase with free BTC is essentially a scam.
8|19: It is not technically feasible to build a legitimate program that just gives you bitcoin in a Coinbase wallet without either owning bitcoin already or using real money to buy it. Bitcoin is not stored or created on Coinbase; Coinbase just keeps track of balances connected to real UTXOs on the blockchain.  What you can code is a convenience tool. For example, if you do cloud mining or run your own mining rig, you could have your mining payouts automatically sent to your Coinbase deposit address. Most mining pools allow setting a payout address in their dashboard. The program in that case is the mining software itself, combined with the pool's payout logic.  Typical flow:  Run mining software pointed to a pool (like stratum+tcp://pooladdress). In the pool account, set your Coinbase BTC address as the payout address. When you earn enough, the pool sends BTC to Coinbase.  The code you write might just manage your configuration or monitor payouts. But again, you are providing hash power (and paying electricity) to earn that BTC. There is no on-demand free-btc-to-Coinbase script that actually works as advertised.
9|19: You cannot programmatically mint free bitcoin into your Coinbase account. Every transaction on the Bitcoin network must be signed by a private key that already controls existing coins or is part of a valid mining block reward. If a script on your computer could just send BTC to a Coinbase wallet without cost, the entire system would collapse.  The realistic things you can code include:  A script that uses the Coinbase API to move BTC between your Coinbase accounts or to external addresses. A bot that takes a portion of your paycheck (after it hits your bank), moves it to Coinbase, and buys BTC, effectively automating savings in bitcoin.  For example, a pseudo-automation:  1. Use your bank's API or a budgeting tool to detect new deposits. 2. When a deposit arrives, call Coinbase's API to buy BTC worth, say, 5% of that amount. 3. Leave that BTC in your Coinbase wallet.  This is about automating your financial behavior, not bypassing the rules of Bitcoin. Any downloadable program that says it can add BTC to your Coinbase is almost certainly trying to steal your credentials or get you to send funds to the attacker.
10|19: If your goal is literally to make a program that sends bitcoin to your Coinbase wallet, the prerequisite is that the program must control some bitcoin to begin with. It might be a wallet application you own, a mining payout system, or an integration with a payment site. But it cannot invent BTC.  A simple, legitimate example is a donation bot: you create a Coinbase BTC address, and the program posts it to your social channels or website and thanks donors automatically.  Very simple Python sketch:  coinbase_address = "YOUR_COINBASE_BTC_ADDRESS"  print("If you want to support me, send BTC to:") print(coinbase_address)  # You could extend this by using a blockchain explorer API # to check when new transactions to that address appear and # then trigger a thank-you email or message.  When someone actually sends BTC to that address, Coinbase credits your wallet. The program only facilitates the process. Anything marketed as a tool that injects bitcoin into your Coinbase account without someone else losing it or without a legitimate transfer or purchase is not real and should be avoided.
